draft.title: Rounding errors in repeated calculations
card: Rounding changes a number a little. If you round early and use the rounded number again, the small change is carried into every later step.
Example: 10 ÷ 3 × 3. Round 10 ÷ 3 to 3.3 first and you get 3.3 × 3 = 9.9. The true answer is 10.
The more steps that use the rounded value, the more the small errors can build up.
Keep the full calculator value through every step, and round only the final answer.
draft.remember: Round only at the end, so small errors do not build up.

a.q: What is the best way to find 20 ÷ 3 × 6 correct to 1 decimal place?
opts: Keep the full value of 20 ÷ 3, then round the final answer
Round 20 ÷ 3 to 1 decimal place, then multiply by 6
Round 20 ÷ 3 to a whole number, then multiply by 6
Round every number in the question before starting
a.why: Keeping the full value means no error is carried into the multiplication, and the answer 40 is exact. Rounding 20 ÷ 3 to 6.7 first gives 40.2, which is already out.

b.q: Tom rounds 100 ÷ 7 to 14.3, then multiplies by 7. What does he get, and why is it off?
opts: 100.1, because he rounded 100 ÷ 7 before multiplying
100.1, because he rounded 100 ÷ 7 after multiplying
100, because rounding a value does not change the result
99.9, because 14.3 is lower than 100 ÷ 7
b.why: 14.3 × 7 = 100.1, but the true answer is 100. The error came from rounding 100 ÷ 7 early, then using the rounded value. In fact 14.3 is higher than 100 ÷ 7, which is about 14.2857.
b.clue: Work out 14.3 × 7, then think about when he rounded.

a.best: Keep the full value of 20 ÷ 3, then round the final answer
